bib.title: WebShop: Towards Scalable Real-World Web Interaction with Grounded Language Agents
bib.venue: 36th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2022)

read.skipped: reference list skimmed for lineage only

question: Can a large-scale, automatically scored, real-world-language web shopping environment be built so that grounded language agents can be trained and evaluated without human feedback in the loop?
hypothesis: A simple rule heuristic cannot resolve noisy options, explore strategically or generate searches, so its score and success rate should be low; pretrained-language IL plus RL should do better but stay far below humans.
contributions: WebShop: simulated e-commerce site with 1,181,436 scraped Amazon products and 12,087 crowd-sourced instructions, with an automatic reward function
Over 1,600 human demonstrations and a human-vs-agent analysis
IL, RL and IL+RL agents using pretrained BART, BERT and ResNet, compared with a rule baseline
Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to amazon.com and ebay.com

method.summary: WebShop is a Flask/OpenAI Gym environment with a BM25 (Pyserini) search engine over scraped Amazon products. The agent gets a text instruction and issues search and choose actions; reward is computed from hidden attributes, options, price and a type match at purchase. Agents are a BART search generator plus a BERT choice model trained by imitation on human trajectories, optionally fine-tuned with policy-gradient RL.
method.task: goal-directed web shopping (language grounding, sequential decision making)

datasets.name: WebShop products
datasets.size: 1,181,436 products; 670 unique attributes; avg 3.1 attributes and 0.67 options per product; 842,849 unique options
datasets.source: scraped from amazon.com with ScraperAPI, 5 categories (fashion, makeup, electronics, furniture, food)
datasets.preprocessing: duplicate titles or product IDs filtered, no other filtering; attributes mined by TF-IDF bi-grams per category, top 200 per category reviewed manually, pool of 670

datasets.name: WebShop instructions
datasets.size: 12,087 instructions; vocabulary 9,036 words; avg length 15.9 words
datasets.source: Amazon Mechanical Turk, 213 qualified workers, $0.15 per example

datasets.name: Human demonstrations
datasets.size: 1,012 training trajectories (1,421 instruction-search pairs; 9,558 choice samples) plus 54 dev-set trajectories for IL hyperparameter tuning and checkpoint selection; human trajectories also for all 500 test instructions
datasets.source: 13 MTurk workers in HTML mode, top 7 labelled experts; $0.7 per trajectory

models.name: Rule baseline
models.architecture: search the exact instruction text, buy first result with no options

models.name: IL search generator (BART)
models.architecture: BART seq2seq, instruction to search[...] query

other.decode: beam search, top-5 queries, one chosen at random

models.name: IL choice model (BERT)
models.architecture: 12-layer BERT encoder of observation and each action, cross-attention (Seo et al.) then mean pool, softmax over actions; ResNet-50 image features (512-d, linear to 768-d) concatenated

models.name: IL+RL
models.architecture: choice IL model fine-tuned with policy gradient and a value head tied to BERT; BART frozen, top-10 search generations as action space

models.name: RL (RNN)
models.architecture: same attention layer, one-layer bi-directional GRU hidden 512 replacing the Transformer, plus instruction-action cross attention

training.objective: IL: negative log-likelihood for search (BART) and choice (BERT). RL: L_RL = L_PG + L_value + L_entropy; policy gradient with return-to-go and learned value baseline V(o)
training.optimizer: RL: Adam; IL optimizer not stated
training.batch_size: IL: 1 with 32 gradient accumulation steps; RL: 4 parallel environments, BPTT every 8 steps
training.regularisation: entropy loss to prevent premature convergence (RL)
training.hardware: IL: one RTX 2080 GPU (~10GB); RL BERT: one RTX 3090 (~20GB); RL GRU: one RTX 2080 (~10GB)
training.compute: IL ~2 hours; RL Transformer ~27 hours; RL GRU ~20 hours
training.seeds: 3 trials for Fig 4 and image ablation (Tables 9-10)

other.code_base: IL code adapted from Huggingface glue example (Apache 2.0)

inference.decoding: search: beam search top-5, uniform random pick; choice: sample from policy softmax (top-1 choice degrades)
inference.retrieval: Pyserini BM25 over title+description+overview+options; deterministic; top 50 items over 5 pages of 10

other.observation_mode: models use simple mode; humans use HTML mode

metrics.name: Success Rate (SR)
metrics.definition: portion of instructions where r = 1 (not necessarily the target product y*)

eval.protocol: 500 test instructions, 3 trials for models; sim-to-real on 100 test instructions manually scored with Eq. 1; reward verified by manual re-scoring of 100 average and 100 expert trajectories

availability.code: https://webshop-pnlp.github.io (project site with code, data, demos)

results.claim: Best agent (IL+RL) reaches a task score of 62.4 and 28.7% success on the WebShop test split, well below expert humans.
results.setup: WebShop test split, 500 instructions, IL+RL, 3 trials
results.quote: Further RL ﬁnetuning improves the score to 62.4 while slightly hurting the success rate (29.1% →28.7%)
results.note: Abstract says 29%; the intro and Sec 5.2 say 'best model's success rate (29.1%)' for IL and 28.7% for IL+RL.

results.claim: Expert humans reach 82.1 score and 59.6% SR; the best model's SR is less than half of that.
results.setup: 7 expert workers, HTML mode, 500 test instructions
results.quote: our best model’s success rate (29.1%) is less than half of expert humans (59.6%) and only 60% of the average human (50%)
results.note: Abstract states 59 percent for human expert; intro 59.6%.

results.claim: Rule baseline (search instruction, buy first result) scores 45.6 with 9.6% SR.
results.quote: a heuristic baseline that achieves 45.6 and 9.6%, respectively
results.note: Sec 5.2 says 'a very low success rate of 10%'; Fig 4 prints 9.6.

results.claim: IL scores 59.9, more than the rule baseline on both metrics.
results.setup: IL with BART search + BERT choice
results.note: Table 9 reports IL as 60.56 (1.94) and SR 29.00 (2.42) over 3 trials, a slightly different number.

results.claim: RL fine-tuning makes the agent greedier: trajectory length falls from 9.4 to 4.8 and option score falls from 45.2 to 38.9.
results.quote: but option score drops from 45.2 to 38.9
results.note: Text says length 9.4 to 4.8 while Table 2 prints states 9.4 for IL and 4.5 for IL+RL.

results.claim: Largest human-agent score gap is on options (28 percent).
results.setup: Table 2 score breakdown, human expert vs agents
results.quote: the most signiﬁcant boost comes from the option score (a 28% gap)

results.claim: A Choice oracle (exhaustive option search with access to hidden reward) lifts the rule heuristic SR from 9.6% to 85.4% and human experts from 59.6% to 87.8%; choosing is a major bottleneck.
results.setup: 500 test instructions, oracle given a search query, tries all items and option combinations, hundreds or thousands of steps per episode
results.quote: Choice oracle improves the success rate of rule heuristics from 9.6% to 85.4%, and even the human expert success rate from 59.6% to 87.8% (Table 4)

results.claim: Even with the oracle, the last human search query beats the others, so query quality still matters.
results.setup: Table 4: instruction text 85.4, IL BART 84.2, human first 85.6, human last 87.8
results.quote: the last human search query still outperforms other search queries
results.table: Table 4, column Human expert (last), row Success Rate
results.note: Table 4 columns are garbled in extraction; column assignment inferred from text (85.4 instruction, 87.8 last human).

results.claim: Zero-shot sim-to-real: IL+RL gets 65.9 score / 25% SR on Amazon and 62.3 / 21% on eBay over 100 test instructions, against rule 45.8 / 19% and 31.7 / 7%.
results.setup: models trained on WebShop, no fine-tuning, 100 test instructions, manual scoring by Eq. 1
results.quote: On amazon.com, IL+RL achieves a Score of 65.9 and SR of 25%, outperforming the Rule baseline’s Score of 45.8 and SR of 19% by large margin.
results.note: Human average on Amazon/eBay is printed as 88.0 / 79.7 in text and 88.2 / 79.7 in Table 5. Amazon IL has the highest SR (27%) in Table 5.

results.claim: Human web interaction on Amazon took about 815 seconds per episode versus under 8 seconds for IL and IL+RL.
results.quote: taking on average 815 seconds per episode as opposed to < 8 seconds per episode for our IL and IL+RL models on Amazon

results.claim: Pretrained BERT matters: without language-pretraining of the choice model, SR drops by nearly two-thirds.
results.setup: IL w/o LP Choice vs IL, 3 trials
results.quote: the success rate drops by nearly two-thirds
results.note: Exact bar values only in Fig 4; row-to-bar mapping is ambiguous in the extraction.

results.claim: RL trained directly from pretrained BERT, without IL warm start, does worse than the rule baseline.
results.quote: the performance is even worse than the rule baseline

results.claim: Automatic reward tracks human re-scoring: Pearson 0.856 on average-worker trajectories and 0.773 on expert trajectories; automatic score is a lower bound.
results.setup: 100 average-worker and 100 expert trajectories re-scored manually; automatic 74.9 vs manual 76.3 (average), 81.5 vs 89.9 (expert)
results.quote: For the average trajectories, the automatic task score was 74.9 and our manual score was 76.3 with a Pearson correlation of 0.856.

results.claim: 87.0% of automatic scores are within 10% of the manual score for average workers.
results.note: Sentence breaks across a page; quote is the in-text fragment.

results.claim: Human worker variance is large: eight evaluators averaged 75.5 score / 50.0% SR; best 87.4 / 69.5%, worst 45.8 / 10%.
results.quote: The 8 participants achieve an overall score of 75.5 and a success rate of 50.0%

results.claim: Using top-1 search instead of random top-5 slightly improves IL (60.56 to 61.96 score) while top-1 choice hurts a lot (45.10).
results.table: Table 9, row IL (top-1 search), column Score

results.claim: Removing images barely changes IL performance (60.3 vs 60.6) but cuts variance.
results.table: Table 10, row IL (w/o image), column Score

results.claim: Searching the raw instruction finds the target item on the first results page (ranks 1-10) nearly 1/3 of the time and not in the top 50 more than half the time.
results.setup: WebShop search engine, instruction as query, Fig 2
results.quote: the corresponding item appears in the ﬁrst search page (rank 1-10) nearly 1/3 of the time

limits: i.i.d. split only; no generalisation split by category (authors say future work can do this)
Exact-match reward under-scores products: human re-score is always >= automatic score; synonyms not matched
A reward of 1 does not require the target product; many items can satisfy an instruction
Instruction attributes are generic and options can be too specific so agents can cheat on option cues; reviews and images are unused in the task
Data biased to US/English Amazon; attribute labelling manual and possibly biased
Human trajectories vary widely; some workers are impatient so the human baseline is noisy
Sim-to-real eval is 100 instructions, manually scored; agent could only do search and open item on the real site, buy was held within the interface
No LLM prompting baselines (2022); models are small BERT/BART agents, so numbers have dated

terms.definition: agent with access to hidden reward, attributes and options that exhaustively tries every result item and option combination for a given search query
